name: Solomon
bio:
Solomon was a son born to David in Jerusalem, first named simply among his many brothers (2 Samuel 5:14) — the child who would grow up to inherit David's throne, build the temple the LORD promised through Nathan, and become Israel's most celebrated king for his wisdom and wealth.

Solomon's birth is told in full after David's affair with Bathsheba and the death of their first child, born while Uriah was still her husband. After that infant's death, David comforted Bathsheba, and she conceived again; the son she bore was named Solomon, and the LORD loved him, sending word through the prophet Nathan that he should also be called Jedidiah, meaning "beloved of the LORD" (2 Samuel 12:24-25) — a quiet sign of grace at the start of a story shadowed by his parents' sin.

While Solomon was still young, David called him aside and explained why he, David, would not be the one to build the LORD's temple: he had shed too much blood in his many wars, so the LORD had reserved that honor for a son of peace — Solomon himself, whose very name reflected the rest God would give Israel in his days. David charged him to build the house with courage and fidelity to the LORD's law, and had already stockpiled enormous quantities of gold, silver, bronze, iron, and cedar so that Solomon would not have to start from nothing (1 Chronicles 22).

David later repeated this charge publicly before all Israel's assembled leaders, explaining that God had chosen Solomon from among his many sons, and handed him the detailed architectural plan for the temple's rooms, courts, and furnishings along with the exact weights of gold and silver for its vessels — a design David said the LORD had put in writing and given him to understand by the Spirit. He urged Solomon to serve the LORD wholeheartedly, be strong and courageous, and finish the work, assuring him that the priests, Levites, and all the people would stand ready to help (1 Chronicles 28).

As David grew old, his son Adonijah tried to seize the throne for himself, but Nathan and Bathsheba moved David to honor his earlier oath that Solomon would reign; David had Solomon anointed king at Gihon by Zadok and Nathan while he himself still lived, ensuring a peaceful transfer of power (1 Kings 1). David then gave vast personal wealth toward the temple and called on Israel's leaders to give as willingly, leading the whole assembly in a prayer of thanksgiving before a second, fully public anointing of Solomon the next day, with great sacrifices and celebration; Zadok was anointed priest at the same time, and all Israel's leaders and even David's own sons submitted themselves to the new king (1 Chronicles 29:1-25). Before he died, David charged Solomon to walk faithfully in the LORD's ways and to deal wisely with the unfinished business of his reign — bringing Joab to account for his bloodshed, showing continued kindness to Barzillai's family, and settling accounts with Shimei (1 Kings 2:1-9). Solomon's kingdom was established once David died, but Adonijah's request to marry Abishag, David's former attendant, struck Solomon as a renewed bid for the throne; he had Adonijah executed, exiled Abiathar from the priesthood, had Benaiah strike down Joab at the altar where he had fled for sanctuary, and ultimately had Shimei put to death for breaking the terms of his pardon — securing the kingdom firmly in his own hands (1 Kings 2:10-46).

## 📖 Core Story: The Gift of Wisdom and the Judgment of Two Mothers

With his kingdom secure, Solomon made an alliance with Pharaoh of Egypt by marrying his daughter, and went to Gibeon, the great high place, to offer a thousand burnt offerings. There the LORD appeared to him in a dream and said, "Ask for whatever you want me to give you." Solomon, calling himself "only a little child" unsure how to carry out his duties, asked not for long life, riches, or the death of his enemies, but for "a discerning heart to govern your people and to distinguish between right and wrong" (1 Kings 3:1-9). The LORD was pleased with the request and granted him a wise and discerning heart unmatched by anyone before or since, along with riches and honor he had not even asked for, promising long life as well if Solomon continued walking in his ways (1 Kings 3:10-14). Chronicles' retelling adds that the altar at Gibeon on which Solomon made his thousand offerings was the very bronze altar Bezalel had built for the tabernacle generations earlier, and that Solomon explicitly asked God to establish the promise given to David and for wisdom to govern a people "as numerous as the dust of the earth" (2 Chronicles 1:1-13).

Solomon's wisdom was soon tested directly. Two prostitutes came before him, each claiming to be the mother of the same living infant, the other child having died in the night. With no witnesses and no way to prove either claim, Solomon called for a sword and ordered the living child cut in two, one half given to each woman. The true mother, her heart overflowing with love for her son, begged the king to give the baby to the other woman rather than see him killed; the false claimant, unmoved, said to divide him. Solomon then gave the child to the woman who had pleaded for his life, declaring her the true mother. When all Israel heard of this judgment, they held the king in awe, recognizing that the wisdom of God was in him to administer justice (1 Kings 3:16-28).

## 📖 Core Story: A Kingdom at Its Height

Solomon organized his kingdom with princes over the priesthood, the scribes, the army, and the household, and divided the land into twelve districts, each supplying provisions for the royal court one month a year — a daily provision so vast it included thirty measures of flour, sixty of meal, and dozens of cattle, sheep, and game (1 Kings 4:1-23). His rule extended over all the kingdoms from the Euphrates to the border of Egypt, and Judah and Israel lived in safety and abundance throughout his reign, "each man under his own vine and fig tree" (1 Kings 4:24-25). God gave Solomon wisdom, insight, and breadth of understanding "as measureless as the sand on the seashore," surpassing the wisdom of the East and of Egypt; he composed three thousand proverbs and over a thousand songs, and spoke with authority on plant life, animals, birds, reptiles, and fish, drawing visitors from every nation who came to hear his wisdom (1 Kings 4:29-34).

## 📖 Core Story: Building the Temple

Solomon made a treaty with Hiram, king of Tyre, who supplied cedar and juniper timber cut by his skilled Sidonian woodsmen, in exchange for wheat and olive oil; Solomon conscripted a labor force of thirty thousand Israelites under Adoniram, along with seventy thousand carriers and eighty thousand stonecutters, to prepare the materials (1 Kings 5). In the fourth year of his reign, 480 years after the exodus from Egypt, Solomon began building the temple, a structure overlaid throughout with gold, carved with cherubim, palm trees, and flowers, with two olive-wood cherubim overshadowing the inner sanctuary where the ark would rest; quarried stone was so fully prepared beforehand that no hammer, chisel, or iron tool was heard at the building site itself. The LORD told Solomon that if he walked in his statutes and commands, he would fulfill his promise to dwell among Israel and never forsake his people. The temple took seven years to complete (1 Kings 6). Solomon spent thirteen years more building his own palace complex, including the Hall of the Forest of Lebanon and a throne hall for judging cases, using the same costly stone and cedar (1 Kings 7:1-12). He brought in a skilled bronze craftsman, also named Hiram, from Tyre, who cast the temple's two great bronze pillars, Jachin and Boaz, the enormous bronze Sea resting on twelve bronze oxen, and all its other bronze furnishings, along with golden altars, tables, lampstands, and utensils for the sanctuary itself (1 Kings 7:13-51).

## 📖 Core Story: The Temple's Dedication

Solomon assembled all of Israel's elders and tribal leaders to bring the ark of the covenant up from Zion into the newly built temple, sacrificing sheep and cattle beyond counting along the way. As the priests set the ark in the Most Holy Place beneath the wings of the cherubim and withdrew, a cloud filled the temple, so thick with the glory of the LORD that the priests could not continue their service — and Solomon declared that the LORD had chosen to dwell in the thick darkness he had now built him a house for forever (1 Kings 8:1-13). Turning to bless the assembled congregation, Solomon recounted how the LORD had kept his promise to David that his son would build the temple, then knelt on a bronze platform he had built in the courtyard, spreading his hands toward heaven, and prayed a long, sweeping dedication prayer (2 Chronicles 6:12-13): that the LORD would hear prayers offered toward this house in every circumstance — sin, defeat, drought, famine, siege, or exile — and even the prayers of foreigners who came from distant lands because they had heard of his great name, so that all the peoples of the earth might know that the LORD is God and there is no other (1 Kings 8:14-61). Chronicles closes the prayer with a final appeal echoing the Psalms, asking the LORD to rise up and enter his resting place together with the ark, clothe his priests with salvation, and remember his covenant mercies to David (2 Chronicles 6:40-42). Solomon and all Israel then dedicated the temple with an overwhelming sacrifice of 22,000 cattle and 120,000 sheep, and kept a joyful two-week festival before sending the people home, blessing the king and rejoicing over everything the LORD had done for David and for Israel (1 Kings 8:62-66).

## 📖 Core Story: Wealth, the Queen of Sheba, and Growing Unfaithfulness

After Solomon finished the temple and his palace, the LORD appeared to him a second time, as at Gibeon, promising to consecrate the temple forever and establish his throne if he walked faithfully as David had — but warning that if Solomon or his descendants turned to other gods, the LORD would cut Israel off from the land and reject the temple itself, making Israel a byword among the nations (1 Kings 9:1-9). Solomon continued building extensively, fortifying cities such as Hazor, Megiddo, and Gezer, and his trading fleet, sailing with Hiram's experienced sailors, brought back thirteen tons of gold from Ophir alone (1 Kings 9:10-28).

When the queen of Sheba heard of Solomon's fame, she came to Jerusalem with a great caravan of spices, gold, and precious stones to test him with hard questions; Solomon answered everything she asked, and when she saw his wisdom, his palace, his officials, and his offerings at the temple, she was overwhelmed, declaring that not even half of his greatness had been told to her. She gave him gold and spices in great abundance, and Solomon gave her all she desired before she returned to her own country (1 Kings 10:1-13). Solomon's wealth grew immense: 666 talents of gold came to him yearly, and he made golden shields and an ivory throne overlaid with gold, flanked by lions, unlike any in any other kingdom; silver became as common as stones in Jerusalem, and he amassed fourteen hundred chariots and twelve thousand horsemen. "Solomon was greater in riches and wisdom than all the other kings of the earth," and the whole world sought audience with him (1 Kings 10:14-29).

## 📖 Core Story: Solomon's Fall into Idolatry

But Solomon loved many foreign women — Moabite, Ammonite, Edomite, Sidonian, and Hittite — despite the LORD's explicit warning that intermarriage with these nations would turn Israel's heart after other gods. He had seven hundred wives and three hundred concubines, and as he grew old, they turned his heart away; he followed Ashtoreth, the goddess of the Sidonians, and Molek, the detestable god of the Ammonites, even building high places for Chemosh of Moab and Molek on the hill facing Jerusalem for his foreign wives to worship their own gods. The LORD, who had appeared to Solomon twice, was angry that his heart had turned away despite this direct command, and declared that he would tear the kingdom from Solomon, though not in his own lifetime, for David's sake — and would leave his son one tribe, for the sake of David and of Jerusalem (1 Kings 11:1-13). The LORD then raised up adversaries against Solomon, including Hadad the Edomite and Rezon of Damascus, and, within his own court, the prophet Ahijah told Solomon's official Jeroboam that the LORD would give him ten of the twelve tribes; when Solomon sought to kill him for it, Jeroboam fled to Egypt and stayed there until Solomon died (1 Kings 11:14-40).

Solomon reigned forty years in Jerusalem over all Israel, and when he died he was buried in the City of David; his son Rehoboam succeeded him on a throne that was, because of Solomon's unfaithfulness, already destined to be torn apart (1 Kings 11:41-43).

His rise to the throne, his reign, and his legacy unfold in detail across the rest of Samuel, 1 Kings, and 1-2 Chronicles.
